newsitem.title: USA: UPS, Teamsters resume marathon talks.
newsitem.headline: UPS, Teamsters resume marathon talks.

text.p: UPS and the Teamsters union held a second consecutive day of talks Friday amid signs of some progress toward settling the 12-day-old strike crippling the nation's largest package carrier.

The first concrete evidence of possible progress came early Friday morning when a spokesman for a federal mediator said the two sides had recessed after 17 hours of talks to analyze data and do complex computations. That often means the parties are considering new proposals.

"They are working hard on the issues," Susan King, a spokeswoman for Labor Secretary Alexis Herman, said late Thursday. UPS and the union reconvened face-to-face talks around 10 a.m.(1400 GMT) Friday.

United Parcel Service made no comment as the talks continued. But a union source was cautious about the direction of the negotiations. "There's been very little movement if at all," the source told Reuters early Friday.
Some 185,000 UPS workers have been on strike since Aug. 4 to demand full-time status and benefits for some of the company's many part-time employees. The walkout is one of the biggest this decade.
The strike is putting increasing pressure on both sides.

The company estimates it is losing $300 million a week, putting its losses so far at about $500 million. UPS carried 80 percent of the small packages in the United States before the strike. It has tried to keep priority deliveries such as medical supplies going with management help but its volume has shrunk to about 10 percent of normal.
The strikers themselves are getting help from other unions, but finding it tough to live on $55-a-week strike benefits.

Opinion polls suggest the public sympathizes more with the strikers than with the company. Many small businesses are feeling the pinch of being unable to deliver their goods. Some have laid off workers or lost substantial business.

UPS competitors have rushed to try to fill the void. The U.S. Postal Service said Friday it would continue Sunday deliveries in some areas of the United States to handle increased mail volume as a result of the strike.
The volume of packages handled by Federal Express Corp. and DHL Worldwide Express has surged since the strike.

Until late this week, UPS took a hard line in the negotiations, insisting that the union put the company's last contract offer to a membership vote and calling on President Bill Clinton to use his powers to stop the strike.
But Clinton has refused to intervene and UPS appeared to soften its stance Thursday, suggesting its "final" offer was negotiable.
While Clinton has stayed out of the dispute, his Labor Secretary has played a prominent role in trying to keep the two sides talking.
She has been present at the hotel where the negotiations are taking place under the guidance of a federal mediator. Aides said she is nearby in case she is needed for consultation.
"Nobody's going to walk out on the secretary," said one source close to Herman.
